design_detail: Government-commissioned evidence update, the eighth and final report in a series of 'independent reports' first commissioned by Public Health England and, since October 2021, by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID); eight authors at King's College London 'with a group of international collaborators'. The full report is a 1,468-page PDF. This card is built from the two HTML pages that GOV.UK publishes: the Main findings page and the Summary page, which has one section for each of 16 chapters. The report contains two systematic reviews run by the authors (the health risks of vaping, with a literature search cut-off of July 2021, and vaping harm perceptions), a summary of a 2022 Cochrane review of heated tobacco products, and survey chapters on smoking and vaping among young people and adults in England (ASH-Y, ITC Youth, ONS Annual Population Survey, Smoking Toolkit Study, ASH-Adult, ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey) together with NHS Digital, National Poisons Information Service and London Fire Brigade data. For each health chapter the authors first restate earlier reports (their own 2018 review for Public Health England, the National Academies 2018 report and the Committee on Toxicity), then add the findings of their own review, run meta-analyses 'wherever possible' by an algorithm (Table 6 of Chapter 2 of the full report, not seen) and word conclusions with the National Academies' levels of evidence (61 evidence statements, listed in the full report). The review questions, as printed in Chapters 7 and 8, are: what effect vaping has on biomarkers associated with the risk of cancer, respiratory, cardiovascular and other conditions; and what effect vaping has on disease outcomes in people who already have a health condition. Two topics were left out because Cochrane reviews cover them: the link between vaping and later smoking, and whether vaping helps people who smoke to quit. AMSTAR 2 is used because the Summary states systematic reviews and a search cut-off (Chapter 1, Issues addressed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 2, 4th paragraph; Chapter 16, Overall implications, 6th paragraph). The Methods that AMSTAR 2 asks about are in the unread PDF, so most items are marked no-information (see risk of bias).
can_establish: What the authors conclude, at what stated level of evidence, about exposure to nicotine and toxicants and about biomarkers of potential harm in people who vape, compared with people who smoke and with people who use no nicotine; how many and what kinds of studies sit under each conclusion (counts per chapter, share from the UK, cross-sectional against longitudinal against cross-over designs); the pooled percentage differences the authors print for individual biomarkers; where the authors found no human studies at all (people with an existing cardiovascular condition or cancer, clinical heart disease, stroke, subclinical atherosclerosis); the follow-up periods of the studies reviewed (single use to 7 days; 8 days to 12 months; little beyond); survey prevalence of smoking and vaping in England to 2022; counts of poisonings, fires and explosions.
cannot_establish: The risk of any disease from vaping, or its size, against people who smoke or people who use no nicotine: the Summary pages contain no disease-incidence data and no pooled risk estimate, and the 'at least 95% less harmful' figure they repeat is a judgement that the pages do not derive. Effects of vaping beyond about 12 months. Whether lower biomarker levels mean lower disease risk. The number of records screened and excluded, the search strategy, the risk-of-bias tools and per-study ratings, the confidence intervals and numbers of studies behind each pooled percentage, and the wording of the 61 evidence statements (all in the unread PDF). Anything published after July 2021, including the PATH Study cohort report on cardiovascular disease (card sc_berlowitz_2022). Whether cohort or cross-sectional studies of heart, lung or other disease in the general population were searched for at all, since neither review question asks for them (see reporting issues).

sample.recruitment: Databases, search terms, screening method and the flow of records are not described in the Summary or Main findings pages. The pages give the search cut-off for the health chapters (July 2021, Chapter 16, Overall implications) and the two review questions. For the health chapters the authors say they first summarised earlier reports (the 2018 review for Public Health England, the National Academies 2018 report and the Committee on Toxicity of Chemicals in Food, Consumer Products and the Environment), then presented their own review. Survey chapters use national surveys of people in England (Chapters 3 and 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not given on the pages read. Visible scope decisions: nicotine vaping only (cannabis vaping excluded); the relationship between vaping and later smoking, and the effectiveness of vaping for stopping smoking, not reviewed (Chapter 1, Issues addressed); the second review question (disease outcomes in people with existing conditions) found no cardiovascular studies and, for exposure biomarkers, none that tested differences between groups (Chapters 7 and 11).
sample.demographics: Not summarised for the health review. Chapter 7 compares young people with adults only for nicotine, volatile organic compounds and tobacco-specific nitrosamines (same direction in young people, smaller nitrosamine difference); Chapter 11 says the evidence gives no insight by sex, age or ethnicity. Chapter 7 says most people who vape previously smoked for a long time (Implications, Improvements in definitions needed).
sample.selection_effects: The health search stops in July 2021, so the PATH Study cardiovascular report (2022) and later work are outside it. The UK supplied a minority of studies (nicotine 5 of 60; volatile organic compounds 5 of 24; nitrosamines 3 of 28; other toxicants 1 of 9; carbon monoxide 3 of 33; metals 0 of 10; secondhand 0 of 6; respiratory 3 of 25; heart rate 4 of 31; blood pressure 3 of 30). Many exposure findings come from tobacco-industry-funded confinement trials of up to 7 days (Chapter 7, Implications). Most studies were short: 27 of 41 cardiovascular studies were cross-over or acute-exposure designs. The review questions ask about biomarkers and about people with existing conditions, so studies of new disease in the general population may have been outside the question (reader's inference from the printed questions; the inclusion criteria were not seen). The authors say most studies in the US used nicotine concentrations above the legal threshold in the UK and EU (Chapter 11, Implications).

exposure.measurement: Vaping as defined by each included study, which differ: people who only vape, people who vape and also smoke, occasional and daily vaping, vaping with and without nicotine; most studies did not check smoking or vaping status with a biological test (Chapter 8, Issues caused by differences between studies). Chapter 7 says some studies grouped people who vape and smoke, occasional vaping and exclusive daily vaping as one group.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Inhaled aerosol. Study conditions as the Summary describes them: single sessions and acute exposure (single use to 7 days); short to medium-term follow-up (8 days to 12 months); long-term (more than 12 months) rarely; confinement trials of up to 7 days; ad libitum use in some studies; devices and e-liquids varied (device type, nicotine form and concentration, flavour). The longest follow-ups named: 4 months for pulse wave velocity (Chapter 11) and up to 5 years in one COPD cohort (Chapter 10).
exposure.polysubstance: Groups differ in how they treat dual use (vaping and smoking): some studies pool it with exclusive vaping, which the authors say can confound results. Some imaging and bronchoscopy studies included people who smoked tobacco or cannabis in the vaping groups (Chapter 10). Past smoking: 'Historical tobacco use can greatly affect many of the biomarkers' and, the authors say, most people who vape previously smoked for a long time; they call for studies of people who vape and have never smoked (Chapter 8, Implications).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Some studies did not allow adequate wash-out for biomarkers with long half-lives (Chapter 7, Evidence reviewed). The authors recommend biological verification of status, for example exhaled carbon monoxide or the nitrosamine metabolite NNAL (Chapter 7, Implications). Compliance with allocation was not always verified (Chapter 11, Implications).

comparison.controls: Relative comparisons: people who vape against people who smoke. Absolute comparisons: people who vape against people who use no tobacco or nicotine. Also nicotine against non-nicotine vaping (heart rate, blood pressure), and before-and-after comparisons in people who switched from smoking to vaping (interventional and longitudinal studies). The authors note that people who stopped smoking long ago, with and without vaping, and people who vape and have never smoked, are rarely compared (Chapter 7 and Chapter 10, Implications).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; many included studies were cross-sectional and unmatched.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Past smoking history is the main confounder named for exposure and many harm biomarkers; for 8-isoprostane, longer smoking history, older age and female sex; for volatile organic compounds, household products, diet and place of living (urban or rural). Studies without a group that uses no nicotine 'cannot clearly distinguish' the effects of vaping or smoking on many biomarkers (Chapter 8, Implications).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking of tobacco or cannabis within vaping groups is noted for imaging studies (Chapter 10). Other drug use is not discussed on the pages read.

outcomes.instruments: Biomarkers of exposure: nicotine and its metabolites; urinary metabolites of volatile organic compounds (the acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA, the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA, the 1,3-butadiene metabolite MHBMA); tobacco-specific nitrosamines (NNAL, NAB, NAT, NNN); carboxyhaemoglobin and exhaled carbon monoxide; metals; polyaromatic hydrocarbons. Biomarkers of potential harm: LDL and HDL cholesterol, 8-isoprostane, sNOX2-dp, malondialdehyde, 8-OHdG; white cell count, C-reactive protein, interleukins, TNF-alpha, sICAM-1, fibrinogen; flow-mediated dilation, selectins, nitric oxide, microvesicles; platelet activation; spirometry, exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), impulse oscillometry, imaging and bronchoscopy; heart rate, blood pressure, pulse wave velocity, oxygen saturation; gene expression and DNA methylation. Poisonings, fires and explosions from service data; perception items from surveys.
outcomes.validity_norms: Per-study risk-of-bias ratings are not printed in the pages read. Words used for some sets: 2 secondhand-exposure studies 'at serious risk of bias' and 3 oxygen-saturation studies 'at critical risk of bias' (Chapter 11), risk of bias 'high for all' harm-perception studies (Chapter 15); the tool is not named (the words suggest a ROBINS-I-style scale; reader's inference). The authors say ranges at which biomarkers of potential harm become clinically relevant predictors of disease still need to be developed (Chapter 8, Implications).
outcomes.operationalization: Conclusions are worded with the National Academies' levels of evidence (conclusive, substantial, moderate, limited, insufficient, no available evidence), which Chapter 16 says 'broadly follow' that report and involve 'a great deal of expert judgement' by the authors. These words describe how sure the authors are of a direction of effect; they do not give its size.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable. 61 evidence statements are the nearest count of conclusions (they include harm perceptions and heated tobacco products); their wording is in the unread PDF.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled percentage differences as printed, people who vape against people who smoke, without intervals, numbers of studies per estimate or model type: acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71% lower; acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%; 1,3-butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83%; NNAL 58%; NAB 87%; NAT 94%; NNN 90%. Nicotine and metabolites: 5 meta-analyses, no significant difference; blood carboxyhaemoglobin: 2 meta-analyses, significantly lower. Against people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers significantly higher (4 meta-analyses), tobacco-specific nitrosamines significantly higher (3, cross-sectional), volatile organic compounds not significantly different in 10 meta-analyses except CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study). Heart rate, blood pressure and inflammation markers: directions only (Chapters 8 and 11).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level. The authors name confounders for specific biomarkers (see comparison); the Summary does not say which included studies adjusted for what.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Chapter 7 refers to 'our 2 review protocol questions', so a protocol existed; whether it was registered, where, and any deviations are not stated on the pages read. Chapter 16 recommends pre-registration of study protocols and analysis plans for primary research.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be checked from the pages read: no flow of records, no list of excluded studies, no statement on publication bias. Per-chapter study counts overlap (a study can appear under several biomarker groups), so the total number of included studies cannot be derived.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level. The authors describe many included studies as small (asthma, COPD, imaging) and suggest Bayes factor analysis to judge the strength of evidence from small studies (Chapter 10, Implications).

interpretation_gap.results_show: As of a July 2021 search: in pooled comparisons, biomarkers of exposure to many toxicants and carcinogens are lower in people who vape than in people who smoke (by 58% to 94% for the individual markers whose percentages are printed), but nicotine and its metabolites do not differ significantly in the five pooled comparisons, and nicotine, nitrosamine and acrylonitrile markers are higher than in people who use no nicotine. Biomarkers of potential harm are mixed or insufficient; most studies are short (27 of 41 cardiovascular studies were cross-over or acute-exposure designs) and the longest follow-ups are 4 months (pulse wave velocity) and one COPD cohort followed up to 5 years. The review found no human studies of clinical heart disease, stroke or atherosclerosis (Chapter 11) and none in people with an existing cardiovascular condition or a cancer history (Chapters 9 and 11); the cancer evidence it reviews is biomarker-based. Lung-function and COPD improvements after switching rest on one small cohort reported twice.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Main findings page says that in the short and medium term vaping poses 'a small fraction of the risks of smoking' and is 'not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked', and that 'better-run studies' of short- and medium-term risks 'found no major causes of concern'. Chapter 16 says the earlier 'at least 95% less harmful' estimate 'remains broadly accurate' for the short and medium term, adding that such summaries 'can be simplistic and misinterpreted'. Chapters 9 to 11 move from lower exposure to statements about disease: policies that support switching 'may have relevant outcomes for cancer prevention'; switching is 'likely to slow down the development of respiratory diseases'; cardiovascular risk is 'expected to be much less' than smoking. Gaps: (1) no calculation links the biomarker reductions (58% to 94%) to a figure of 95%, or any biomarker to a disease risk; (2) 'better-run studies' is not defined on the pages read, and the chapters themselves say most studies had methodological concerns and rate lung-function evidence insufficient; (3) 'conclusive' describes the direction of lower exposure, from follow-up of up to 12 months and many tobacco-industry-funded confinement trials of up to 7 days; (4) 'no available evidence' for clinical outcomes may reflect the review questions and the July 2021 cut-off as well as the literature. The authors do say the extent of cardiovascular risk 'remains uncertain' and that vaping is not risk-free.

timeline.event: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report (card sc_nasem_2018). This report says the Academies' conclusions are 'generally supported by this review' (Chapter 11) and that there is still no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular outcomes; it restates the Academies' findings before adding its own, so the two are not independent.

Eissenberg and colleagues argue in an editorial that the '95% less harmful' figure, which the authors of this report stated in their 2015 report, came from a 2013 rating exercise by 12 experts and should no longer be relied on (card sc_eissenberg_2020, written by another reader). The Summary pages do not mention that critique and say the figure 'remains broadly accurate' for the short and medium term.

PATH Study cohort report of new respiratory conditions in 21,618 US adults (card sc_xie_2020), published in November 2020, before this review's July 2021 search cut-off. The Summary names no individual study, so whether it was found and screened out is unknown.
PATH Study cohort report on cardiovascular disease in US adults (card sc_berlowitz_2022), published after the July 2021 cut-off and so outside this review.

Banks and colleagues' umbrella and systematic review cites this report as an English review found after its own search, noting that this report found a lack of direct evidence on major clinical outcomes and generally more favourable results for e-cigarettes than for cigarettes (card sc_banks_2023). Both draw on the National Academies report, and the Banks reference list also cites three earlier reports in this series (2018, 2020 and 2021), so agreement between them is not independent replication.

replication.where_it_stands: Not replicated as a review. The central finding (much lower exposure to many smoke toxicants in people who vape than in people who smoke) agrees in direction with the PATH Study cross-sectional analysis and the Cochrane secondary analysis in this batch (cards sc_goniewicz_2018 and sc_hartmann_boyce_2023), with the size of the gap differing by marker (NNAL 58% lower in the pooled figure here against about 98% in PATH; the acrolein metabolite 71% against about 60%; the acrylonitrile metabolite 94% against about 97%). The statements on disease risk are not replicated: no outcome data are reviewed.

funding.funder: Commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (Department of Health and Social Care, England), as the final report in a series first commissioned by Public Health England. The Main findings page and landing page describe the work as independent; no grant number or budget is printed on the pages read.
funding.declared_conflicts: No declaration of interests appears on the pages read (landing page, Main findings, Summary including Authors and citation). Such declarations, if any, would be in the 1,468-page full report, which was not read. The Summary says the series aims 'to inform policies and regulations' and describes the government's smokefree 2030 ambition in Chapter 1.
funding.affiliations_note: Eight authors, with one affiliation printed for the list, King's College London: Ann McNeill, Erikas Simonavičius, Leonie Brose, Eve Taylor, Katherine East, Elizabeth Zuikova, Robert Calder, Debbie Robson; 'a group of international collaborators' is mentioned without names. The Summary says many of the pooled exposure findings came from tobacco-industry-funded trials (Chapter 7, Implications).

what_would_settle_it: A review of this question with a registered protocol, published search strategy, duplicate screening and extraction, a flow diagram and list of excluded studies, named risk-of-bias tools with per-study ratings, and an explicit question on new heart, lung and other disease in people who vape compared with people who smoke and people who use no nicotine, searched beyond July 2021 and kept up to date (the authors themselves recommend a continual updating approach). Independent studies outside confinement, with biological checks of smoking and vaping status, with follow-up of more than 12 months, and including people who vape and have never smoked and people who stopped smoking long ago and do not vape. A worked derivation of the 'at least 95% less harmful' figure from outcome data, or its replacement by outcome-based estimates.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: The two review questions (Chapters 7, 8, 10) name the population (people who vape; people with existing conditions), the exposure, comparators (people who smoke; people who use no nicotine) and outcomes (biomarkers; disease outcomes). The inclusion criteria themselves are in the unread Methods.
Chapter 7 refers to 'our 2 review protocol questions', so a protocol existed; registration, publication and deviations are not stated on the pages read.
The Summary lists the designs found (RCT, cross-over, non-randomised longitudinal, cross-sectional, animal, cell) but not why they were included.
A July 2021 cut-off is stated (Chapter 16); databases, terms, dates and supplementary searches are not on the pages read.
Not stated on the pages read.
Not stated on the pages read.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No flow of records or list of excluded studies on the pages read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Counts, designs and UK share are given per chapter; study-level tables are in the unread PDF.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Risk of bias was assessed and results are given in words (serious, critical, high) for some sets, but the tool and the per-study ratings are not on the pages read.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Chapter 7 notes that many exposure findings came from tobacco-industry-funded confinement trials; whether each study's funder is reported is not visible.
An algorithm for deciding whether to pool is mentioned (Table 6, Chapter 2 of the full report); models, heterogeneity statistics, intervals and numbers of studies per estimate are not printed.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Not stated on the pages read.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Conclusions are repeatedly qualified by risk of bias and design: most studies had methodological concerns that 'limit interpretations of our findings'; 3 oxygen-saturation studies at critical risk of bias allowed no conclusion; all harm-perception studies were at high risk.
Each chapter describes differences in designs, group definitions, biomarkers, samples and exposure periods as the reason few studies could be pooled and results varied by biomarker.
Not mentioned on the pages read.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The commissioning body is named; no declaration of interests for the authors appears on the pages read. It may be in the full report.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: 14 of the 16 items can be judged only from the Methods and appendices of the 1,468-page full report, which was not opened (reading rules: no PDF links). Only items 13 and 14 can be judged from the Main findings and Summary pages, and both are met. No item could be judged no from the pages read. AMSTAR 2 cannot give an overall rating from these pages: the critical items 2, 4, 7, 9, 11 and 15 are unknown, so the true rating could be anywhere from high-confidence to critically-low. The overall word low-confidence is entered only because the schema needs one of the four words; it is a placeholder, not a judgement that the review is weak, and it must be replaced once the Methods are read. What the pages do show: two stated review questions and a protocol; a July 2021 search cut-off; an algorithm for deciding when to pool; meta-analyses where studies were comparable; risk-of-bias results carried into the wording of conclusions; repeated, specific warnings about heterogeneity and about short follow-up. What they do not show is anything that can be checked about the search, selection and extraction. The Summary may be cited for what its authors conclude, at what level of evidence, from what kinds and numbers of studies (as it states them), and for the places where it says no human studies were found; not for the completeness of the search, for the number of studies excluded, for any result dated after July 2021, or as independent confirmation of the National Academies report, which it restates and builds on.

verification.source_read: GOV.UK HTML pages, read 2026-10-18 in a browser tab: the publication landing page (29 September 2022); the Main findings page in full; the Summary page in full (Chapters 1 to 16 and Authors and citation). Not read: the full report (a 1,468-page PDF, not opened under the reading rules), which holds the Methods, Table 6 of Chapter 2, the study-level tables and risk-of-bias ratings, any declarations of interest and the 61 evidence statements. Locators count running-text paragraphs under each heading (headings and list items are not counted; list items are cited as such). Reader 72 cites this card.

key_findings.finding: Aim and scope (Chapter 1). The report calls itself 'the eighth in a series of independent reports', commissioned first by Public Health England and now by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities, and gives the series aim as 'to inform policies and regulations'. Its opening, before any evidence, says vaping products 'can play a vital role in reducing the huge health burden' of smoking. It 'focuses predominantly on the potential health risks of vaping' and leaves two topics to Cochrane reviews: the link between vaping and later smoking (people under 30) and whether vaping helps people who smoke to quit. Vaping products means e-cigarettes and e-liquids intended for nicotine vaping (studies of products without nicotine are labelled as such); the report counts people who regularly use them as people who vape and excludes cannabis vaping.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 › Objective of the report, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 1 › Issues addressed, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 1 › Terminology, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 1 › Issues addressed, the two list items after the 3rd paragraph (the topics not covered)

key_findings.finding: Regulation, adverse reports and surveillance (Chapter 1). Nicotine vaping products in England are regulated under the Tobacco and Related Products Regulations 2016 and must be notified to the medicines regulator (MHRA); no medicinally licensed vaping product existed in the UK. MHRA Yellow Card scheme: 257 reports of adverse reactions between 20 May 2016 and 13 January 2022 (26 since January 2021); 14 judged serious since January 2021; no deaths. The Summary stresses that 'A report is not proof that the reaction was caused by a vaping product'. An analysis of notifications in 2016 to 2017 'found that notified products were unlikely to cause serious harm'. The authors ask that communications about EVALI (the US lung injury outbreak) separate nicotine vaping from vaping contaminated illicit substances.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 › Main findings › Adverse advents, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 1 › Main findings › Regulations and licensing, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 1 › Implications, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Methods (Chapter 2). Surveys: two for young people (ASH-Y, ITC Youth) and four for adults (ONS Annual Population Survey, Smoking Toolkit Study, ASH-Adult, ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey), plus NHS Digital stop-smoking service data and National Poisons Information Service and London Fire Brigade data. The authors 'conducted 2 systematic reviews' (health risks of vaping; vaping harm perceptions) and summarised a recent Cochrane review of heated tobacco products. For the health chapters they first summarised the 2018 Public Health England review, the National Academies 2018 report and the Committee on Toxicity report, then their own review, using an algorithm to decide whether to run meta-analyses (Table 6 of Chapter 2 of the full report, not seen). The health search cut-off was July 2021 (Chapter 16). Chapter 7 refers to 'our 2 review protocol questions'. The databases, search terms, screening process and risk-of-bias tool are not named on the pages read.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 2, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Chapter 7 › Evidence reviewed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 16 › Overall implications, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Young people in England (Chapter 3; school-age surveys, self-reported, collected February 2021 to March 2022; the authors warn that COVID-19 school closures and restrictions may greatly affect conclusions). ASH-Y 2022 (11 to 18 year olds): 6% smoked and 8.6% vaped (4.1% and 4% in 2021); any nicotine use through smoking or vaping 11.1% (6.2% in 2021; 7.7% in 2015); 98.3% of young people who had never smoked were not vaping; 52.8% of those who currently vaped used disposable devices (7.8% in 2021). ITC Youth 2021 (16 to 19 year olds): among those who currently vaped 52.5% felt a little or very addicted, against 83% of those who currently smoked; the authors conclude that dependence on vaping 'appears lower than on smoking for young people' and ask for research on dependence by product and nicotine type. The measures are self-rated feelings of addiction and urges; Chapter 5 says no consensus scale for vaping dependence exists.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 3 › Main findings › Smoking and vaping prevalence, 1st, 4th and 6th paragraphs; Chapter 3 › Main findings › Vaping devices, 1st paragraph; Chapter 3 › Main findings › Perceived addiction and urges to vape, 1st paragraph; Chapter 3 › Implications › Further monitoring and research, 1st paragraph; Chapter 3 › Data collection, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Adults in England (Chapter 4; four surveys, 2020 to 2022, self-reported). Smoking prevalence in 2021 was between 12.7% and 14.9% depending on the survey (13.2% in 2022); vaping prevalence between 6.9% and 7.1% in 2021 (8.3% in 2022, ASH-Adult). In the Smoking Toolkit Study 22% of people who currently smoked, 11.6% of those who used to smoke and 0.6% of those who have never smoked vaped. The share of people who vape who also smoke fell from 91.9% in 2012 to 49.8% in 2020 (Smoking Toolkit Study) and from 73.7% to 31% in 2021 (ASH-Adult), then rose to 51.7% (2021) and 33.4% (2022); the authors put the gap between surveys down to different definitions of smoking status. The share of people currently vaping who had vaped for more than 3 years rose from 23.7% (2018) to 43.7% (2021). Stop-smoking services, April 2020 to March 2021: self-reported short-term success 64.9% for attempts that involved a vaping product and 58.6% for those that did not (service data as printed; no adjustment for who chose a vaping product is described); only 5.2% of supported attempts involved a vaping product.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 4 › Main findings › Smoking and vaping prevalence, 1st, 3rd, 4th and 6th paragraphs; Chapter 4 › Main findings › Length of time vaping, 1st paragraph; Chapter 4 › Main findings › Using vaping to stop smoking, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nicotine (Chapter 5). Pharmacokinetic studies: vaping generally gives lower peak and lower overall nicotine levels than smoking, reached more slowly; exposure rises with higher e-liquid nicotine concentration, nicotine salts, tank or modular devices (against cartridge or disposable models) and longer experience. Biomarker studies (Chapter 7) generally show lower nicotine exposure over the short term (up to 7 days); the authors rate as moderate the evidence of similar exposure in medium to longer-term studies (up to 2 years) and as substantial the evidence of comparable exposure in experienced adults, with supporting evidence of compensatory puffing. Dependence: substantial evidence (from the National Academies, the Committee on Toxicity and the authors' 2018 report) that vaping can produce symptoms of dependence; moderate evidence that risk and severity are lower than for smoking and vary with the product; no consensus scale for measuring vaping dependence. The health effects of nicotine itself are hard to isolate in people because few use non-nicotine products; pulse wave velocity appeared to be affected by nicotine in acute studies; animal and cell studies suggest some adverse effects of unclear relevance to people.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Main findings › Nicotine intake, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Chapter 5 › Main findings › Nicotine dependency, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 5 › Main findings › Health risks, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Flavours (Chapter 6). Three studies found that tobacco-specific nitrosamines and volatile organic compounds fell significantly in people who smoked, or smoked and vaped, and switched to vaping products with different flavours (differences between flavours were not tested); people using fruit-only flavours had higher levels of the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA than people using a single other flavour in one study. In a longitudinal study 6.9% reported an adverse reaction they linked to the flavour used. From 13 cell and 9 animal studies there is 'limited evidence' that some flavourings, particularly cinnamaldehyde and buttery or creamy flavours, can alter cellular responses, but less than tobacco smoke; base liquids without flavourings appeared to have little or no effect; controls often could not separate nicotine or solvents from flavourings. The authors say cinnamaldehyde-containing products 'continue to be a cause of concern'. The Main findings page: 'a lack of evidence on whether flavourings affect health risks'.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 6 › Main findings › Potential toxicants in flavours, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 6 › Implications, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exposure review: design (Chapter 7). Two review questions; no study answered the second for exposure biomarkers (one study of people with self-reported respiratory symptoms did not test differences between groups). Comparisons were relative (against people who smoke) and absolute (against people who use no nicotine). Studies varied in quality and in definitions (for example grouping people who vape and smoke with exclusive vaping, or comparing occasional vaping with daily smoking). Follow-up was single use to 7 days (acute) or 8 days to 12 months; the authors write that 'we were unable to summarise findings on longer term' vaping exposure (more than 12 months), and some studies left too little wash-out for biomarkers with long half-lives. Meta-analyses were run 'wherever possible', but inconsistent designs, biomarker reporting, group definitions and exposure periods meant 'only a few studies' could be pooled.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Evidence reviewed, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 5th, 6th and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Exposure review: nicotine and metabolites (Chapter 7; 60 studies, 5 from the UK). Large variation by design, definitions of vaping and smoking, biomarker and sample type, and exposure duration. Five meta-analyses (1 longitudinal, 4 cross-sectional) of people who vaped and people who smoked at least weekly found no significant difference. Four meta-analyses against people who use no nicotine found significantly higher levels in people who vape ('as expected'). Narrative summaries agree: with more experience of vaping people can reach nicotine levels similar to smoking; levels varied with device characteristics; no discernible difference between adults and adolescents.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Main findings › Nicotine, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Exposure review: volatile organic compounds (Chapter 7; 24 studies, 5 from the UK). Against people who smoke, 15 meta-analyses (4 longitudinal, 11 cross-sectional): most showed significantly lower levels in people who vape, with reductions of 71% for the acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA, 94% for the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA and 83% for the 1,3-butadiene metabolite MHBMA; for formaldehyde and toluene the evidence was inconclusive. Against people who use no nicotine, 10 meta-analyses (all cross-sectional) found no significant difference except for CNEMA, which was over 3 times higher in one study. Young people: broadly the same direction, with differences for individual biomarkers.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Main findings › Volatile organic compounds, 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Exposure review: tobacco-specific nitrosamines (Chapter 7; 28 studies, 3 from the UK). Against people who smoke, 5 meta-analyses (2 longitudinal, 3 cross-sectional) all showed significantly lower levels in people who vape: NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90%. Against people who use no nicotine, 3 cross-sectional meta-analyses all showed significantly higher levels, but the authors write that cross-sectional data 'make it difficult to distinguish' exposure from vaping from previous tobacco use, and that an RCT and a cross-over study indicate nitrosamine metabolite levels might fall to those of people who use no nicotine. Young people: same direction, with a smaller difference between people who vape and people who smoke than in adults.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Main findings › Tobacco specific nitrosamines, 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Exposure review: other toxicants, carbon monoxide, metals and secondhand exposure (Chapter 7). Other potential toxicants (9 studies, 1 from the UK, no meta-analyses): lower in people who vape than in people who smoke and higher than in people who use no nicotine. Carbon monoxide (33 studies, 3 from the UK): 2 meta-analyses against people who smoke both showed significantly lower blood carboxyhaemoglobin; none against people who use no nicotine, but interventional studies suggested exposure in people who switch completely might fall to levels like those of people who use no nicotine. Metals (10 cross-sectional studies, none from the UK, no meta-analyses): relative findings mixed; absolute findings mixed, although most showed higher exposure in people who vape. Secondhand exposure (6 studies, none from the UK): short exposures gave no detectable change in nicotine, volatile organic compound or nitrosamine biomarkers; longer exposures during heavy sustained vaping gave significant increases in nicotine or toxicant metabolites.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Main findings › Other potential toxicants, 1st paragraph; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Carbon monoxide, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Metals, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Secondhand exposure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Exposure review: the authors' reading (Chapter 7, Implications). Compared with smoking, vaping 'leads to a substantial reduction in biomarkers of toxicant exposure', but the degree of any residual risk 'remains unclear', mainly because people who stopped smoking long ago, with and without vaping, and people who have never smoked or vaped, were rarely compared. Most studies had methodological concerns; a lack of difference from people who use no nicotine may reflect insensitive methods, background exposures or truly similar exposure. 'many findings were from tobacco industry-funded RCTs conducted in confinement' for up to 7 days, so independent studies outside confinement and with longer follow-up are needed. Historical tobacco use affects many biomarkers and, the authors say, most people who vape previously smoked for a long time; they ask for strict definitions of exclusive vaping and biological checks of status. They take higher absolute exposure than not using nicotine as a reason for policies to discourage uptake by people who have never smoked.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Implications › Vaping reduces toxicant exposure compared with cigarette smoking, 1st paragraph; Chapter 7 › Implications › Methodological improvements needed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 7 › Implications › Improvements in definitions needed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 7 › Implications › More research needed on biomarkers of exposure among vapers, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 7 › Implications › Lower risks of exposure from vaping than smoking, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers of potential harm across diseases (Chapter 8; 41 unique studies in 43 publications). The authors list differences that obscure conclusions: different biomarkers; different group definitions with smoking or vaping status usually not verified by a biological test; mostly acute exposures (these biomarkers 'take weeks or months to normalise' after people stop smoking); confounding and few controlled studies. Oxidative stress (1 RCT, 6 cross-over, 5 non-randomised longitudinal and 11 cross-sectional studies): no difference in LDL cholesterol; HDL inconsistent; 8-isoprostane mixed; 'limited evidence' for the rest; most studies show no difference from smoking or from not using nicotine. Inflammation (2 RCTs, 3 cross-over, 3 longitudinal, 17 cross-sectional): pooled cross-sectional data show lower C-reactive protein than in people who smoke and similar to people who use no nicotine, and lower sICAM-1 than in people who smoke, but controlled and longitudinal studies did not confirm this; no definite conclusion. Endothelial function (1 RCT, 4 cross-over, 3 longitudinal, 1 cross-sectional; none pooled): acute vaping (with or without nicotine) and acute smoking each reduced flow-mediated dilation in the short term; a single RCT found that 4 weeks of switching from smoking to vaping improved it; no controlled study compared people who vape with people who use no nicotine. Platelet activation (4 studies): no conclusions. The authors' summary: acute vaping 'might cause endothelial dysfunction as much as acute smoking' but switching 'might improve endothelial function in the longer-term'.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 8 › Main findings › Issues caused by differences between studies, 1st paragraph; Chapter 8 › Main findings › Issues caused by differences between studies, 3rd list item; Chapter 8 › Main findings › Oxidative stress, 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs; Chapter 8 › Main findings › Inflammation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 8 › Main findings › Endothelial function, 1st, 3rd and 7th paragraphs; Chapter 8 › Main findings › Platelet biomarkers, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers of potential harm: the authors' reading (Chapter 8, Implications). Research on biomarkers that cut across diseases 'is still at an early stage'; the findings allow a comparison of immediate effects of vaping and smoking, but the effects of long-term vaping matter most for public health. Most studies in the chapter had methodological concerns. Studies without a group that uses no nicotine 'cannot clearly distinguish' the effects of vaping or smoking from other influences (diet, physical activity), so most 'cannot inform us about the medium or long term' risks. The authors call for studies of people who vape and have never smoked, and for ranges at which these biomarkers predict disease.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 8 › Implications › Need for methodological improvements and longer term studies, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Chapter 8 › Implications › Need to distinguish between biomarkers of potential harm from smoking or vaping from other sources, 1st paragraph; Chapter 8 › Implications › Greater clarity on clinical significance, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cancer (Chapter 9). Earlier reports: the National Academies found no available evidence on whether vaping chemicals or behaviour were associated with cancer risk, and the Committee on Toxicity found existing evidence insufficient. This review calls the human literature 'growing (but still modest)'. Biomarkers of exposure to several carcinogens are lower in people who vape than in people who smoke, which the authors call 'conclusive evidence' of lower exposure to many carcinogens responsible for the health risks of smoking. Inflammation and oxidative stress findings show no systematic relationship and are insufficient to draw conclusions. Gene expression and DNA methylation (2 RCTs, 1 longitudinal and 5 cross-sectional studies, none from the UK) are limited by missing smoking comparison groups. No study assessed people with an existing or previous cancer. Cell and animal studies are hard to translate; the authors say they suggest aerosols 'are not benign to people who have never smoked' and that gene-expression changes are smaller than with smoke. The authors state that biomarker studies need longer follow-up to show whether vaping reduces cancer risk compared with smoking, and that supporting complete switching 'may have relevant outcomes for cancer prevention'. No cancer incidence data are presented.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 9 › Main findings › Toxicants and carcinogens, 1st paragraph; Chapter 9 › Main findings › Cancer risks, 1st paragraph; Chapter 9 › Main findings › Inflammation and oxidative stress, 1st paragraph; Chapter 9 › Main findings › Gene and DNA processes, 1st paragraph; Chapter 9 › Main findings › Existing or previous cancer conditions, 1st paragraph; Chapter 9 › Main findings › Cell and animal studies, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 9 › Implications › Longer follow up periods are needed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 9 › Implications › Support smokers to completely switch from smoking to vaping, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Respiratory biomarkers and tests (Chapter 10; 25 studies, 3 from the UK; no meta-analyses). Exposure: 'conclusive evidence' that exposure to most potential respiratory toxicants is significantly lower with vaping than smoking after single use to 7 days and after 8 days to 12 months, and moderate evidence for long-term exposure (more than 12 months); formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive, and one study suggested formaldehyde exposure might rise with compensatory puffing on lower-nicotine e-liquids; no significant difference from people who use no nicotine except the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA. Biomarkers of potential harm (8-isoprostane, inflammation): mixed, so insufficient evidence. All 25 studies included spirometry; the Summary reports no detrimental effect at acute, short-to-medium or long-term exposure, and a clear worsening of lung function in one small study of people who switched back to smoking for 7 days. FeNO (8 studies): mixed, mostly no significant differences. Impulse oscillometry (1 study) needs repeating. Imaging and bronchoscopy (5 studies) were very short-term or confounded by tobacco or cannabis smoking within the vaping groups. The authors conclude there is 'insufficient evidence' from spirometry, FeNO, oscillometry, bronchoscopy and imaging on whether vaping affects lung function after acute, short to medium or long-term exposure, and on acute secondhand vaping.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 10 › Main findings › Biomarkers of respiratory diseases, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Biomarkers of potential harm, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Respiratory tests and imaging, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Asthma, COPD, mental health, cells and animals, and conclusions (Chapter 10). Asthma (4 studies, generally very small): inconclusive on whether lung function and symptoms improve in adults with asthma who switch completely; 'limited evidence that vaping negatively affects lung function among adults with asthma'. COPD: two longitudinal articles from the same group of patients reported significant improvements in some spirometry measures in the group that used vaping products compared with baseline and none in the group that smoked, with small numbers; the authors conclude 'limited evidence' for fewer COPD exacerbations in adults who smoke, have COPD and switch completely, for up to 5 years, and say improvements 'seem mainly to be among participants who switched to exclusive vaping'. Mental health (1 study): no significant change in one spirometry measure; most participants kept smoking. Cells and animals (47 in vitro and 25 animal studies): aerosol may cause airway adverse effects in these models; the responsible constituents are unclear. Conclusions: the literature has grown since the National Academies report and that report's conclusions are supported; differences in designs, diagnoses and measurements in asthma studies 'prevent us from making any conclusions'. Implications: studies of long-term vaping are 'urgently needed'; the one long-term cohort of people who had switched at baseline is described as promising and should be replicated; the authors judge that supporting complete switching 'is likely to slow down the development of respiratory diseases' on limited evidence; it is not clear whether the spirometry changes are large enough to matter clinically.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 10 › Main findings › Asthma, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Mental health, 1st paragraph; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Cell and animal studies, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Conclusions, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Chapter 10 › Implications › Study people who vape over longer periods of time, 1st paragraph; Chapter 10 › Implications › Switching to vaping likely to slow down respiratory disease development, 1st paragraph; Chapter 10 › Implications › Consider respiratory biomarkers before starting studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular biomarkers (Chapter 11). No study was found in people with an existing cardiovascular condition, so the second review question could not be answered. 41 studies of cardiovascular biomarkers of potential harm (27 of them cross-over or acute-exposure designs; mixed quality; no longer-term summary possible; few could be pooled). Heart rate (31 studies, 9 pooled): acutely, vaping raised heart rate less than smoking and, after short exposure, was similar to not using nicotine; no difference between nicotine and non-nicotine vaping (4 cross-over studies pooled); in longer-term comparisons heart rate was lower in people who vape than in people who smoke when the groups were mutually exclusive, and lower than in people who use no nicotine in one pooled cross-sectional analysis but higher in another cross-sectional study. Blood pressure (30 studies, 9 pooled in 10 meta-analyses): acute effects showed no difference between vaping, smoking or neither apart from a small diastolic difference between vaping and not using nicotine; cross-sectional meta-analyses of people with at least 3 months or a year of vaping found lower blood pressure than in people who smoke and no difference from people who use no nicotine (the authors presume most had stopped smoking). Pulse wave velocity (9 studies, none pooled): may fall after a sustained switch, but the longest follow-up was 4 months; rose after acute nicotine vaping but not non-nicotine vaping. Oxygen saturation: 3 studies, all at critical risk of bias, no conclusions. Secondhand exposure: 2 small studies at serious risk of bias, no conclusions. Lipids and inflammation (also Chapter 8): LDL no difference; HDL similar except in large samples of people who use no nicotine, where it was significantly higher; C-reactive protein and sICAM-1 lower than in people who smoke in pooled cross-sectional studies but not confirmed by interventional studies; one RCT found that switching improved flow-mediated dilation after one month.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 11 › Evidence reviewed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Harm specific to cardiovascular disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Heart rate, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Blood pressure, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Peripheral resistance and arterial stiffness, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Oxygen saturation, 1st paragraph; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Secondhand exposure, 1st paragraph; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Cholesterol, 1st paragraph; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Endothelial function, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular disease outcomes, animals and conclusion (Chapter 11). 'As in 2018', there is 'still no available evidence' on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis (carotid intima-media thickness, coronary artery calcification). The National Academies found insufficient evidence of long-term changes in heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac structure and function; this review found hints of long-term changes in animal studies but no human evidence. The Academies' and the Committee on Toxicity's conclusions are described as generally supported. Animals (16 studies) and cells (2 studies): aerosol raised blood pressure and arterial stiffness markers and increased left ventricular mass and wall thickness, with effects 'potentially less than' those of cigarette smoke, inconsistencies between studies and a largely nicotine-dependent pattern; the authors caution about translating these findings to people. Conclusion: 'the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain', though, 'based on the toxicant profile', the risk 'is expected to be much less than that of cigarette smoking'. Implications: 27 of 41 studies were cross-over or acute-exposure designs that cannot answer questions about cardiovascular health outcomes; studies comparing rates of coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease and stroke between people who use no nicotine, people who use tobacco and people who vape are needed; most US studies used nicotine concentrations above the legal threshold in the UK and EU.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 11 › Main findings › Comparisons with other reports, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Cell and animal studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Conclusion, 1st paragraph; Chapter 11 › Implications, 2nd, 3rd and 10th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Other health outcomes (Chapter 12). 15 human dental-health studies and, for other outcomes, 14 human, 31 animal and 1 cell study (oral, ocular, reproductive, allergy, pre-diabetes). Many studies found worse outcomes in people who vaped than in people who did not vape (or smoke) and others found no difference, but large samples were almost exclusively cross-sectional, 'making any causal statements impossible'; definitions of vaping and smoking groups were often confounded. Evidence on reproductive health and pregnancy outcomes 'remains insufficient'. Oral health: recent reviews concluded that vaping would be detrimental for people who have never vaped or smoked and likely beneficial for people who smoke and switch, and no study changed that conclusion. No study examined possible benefits (the Summary names Parkinson's disease as an example). Animal and cell data (31 and 1 studies) are too limited and inconsistent.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 12 › Evidence reviewed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 12 › Main findings › Limitations of the evidence, 1st paragraph; Chapter 12 › Main findings › Reproductive health, 1st paragraph; Chapter 12 › Main findings › Oral or dental health, 1st paragraph; Chapter 12 › Main findings › Cell and animal studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Poisonings, fires and explosions (Chapter 13). Poisonings: in 2021 the National Poisons Information Service received 187 vaping-product enquiries out of 39,594 telephone enquiries, 82 of them involving children aged 5 or under; 2 UK case reports (both intentional; one death); internationally, 20 studies and case reports, mostly young children who accidentally swallowed e-liquid, almost all recovered, 2 child deaths, and 16 deaths outside the UK where exposure was intentional or unknown. Fires: London Fire Brigade, January 2017 to October 2021: 5,706 fires caused by cigarettes and lighters against 15 caused by vaping products; no injuries or deaths from vaping fires, against 676 injuries and 46 deaths from cigarette fires. Explosions: 'serious but very rare'; 2 UK case reports (4 people, no deaths) and 23 reports abroad (1 death); a device carried in a trouser pocket was the commonest cause.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 13 › Main findings › Poisonings, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 13 › Main findings › Fires, 1st paragraph; Chapter 13 › Main findings › Explosions, 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Heated tobacco products (Chapter 14). Use in England is rare: 0.3% of 11 to 18 year olds (ASH-Y 2021) and 0.3% to 0.5% of adults currently used them; 1.8% of adults had ever used them. The Summary relays a 2022 Cochrane review: no studies of heated tobacco for stopping smoking; moderate-certainty evidence of lower toxicant and carcinogen exposure than continuing to smoke, and moderate to very low certainty of higher exposure than abstinence; some evidence of better FEV1 after switching than continuing to smoke; insufficient evidence on adverse events. The authors call for research independent of manufacturers.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 14 › Main findings › Use of heated tobacco products in England, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Chapter 14 › Main findings › Cochrane review, 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Chapter 14 › Implications, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Harm perceptions (Chapter 15). In 2021, 44.7% of 11 to 18 year olds (ASH-Y) accurately perceived vaping as less harmful than smoking, 32.4% thought the harms about the same, 3.6% more harmful and 19.3% did not know; among adults who smoke (Smoking Toolkit Study) 34.1% accurately perceived vaping as less harmful, 32.1% about the same, 11.9% more harmful and 22% did not know. 13.9% of adults who smoke or vape (ASH-Adult) correctly said that none or a small amount of smoking's risk came from nicotine. A systematic review of 32 articles (29 studies) found that information about the reduced harms of vaping relative to smoking raised the perception that vaping is less harmful, information about absolute harms raised perceptions that vaping is harmful, and the US EVALI outbreak raised harm perceptions, including inaccurate ones relative to smoking; 21 studies found that perceptions predicted later vaping and, in limited evidence, smoking behaviour. The Summary states 'Risk of bias was high for all included studies'.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 15 › Main findings › Young people’s harm and other perceptions of vaping in England, 1st paragraph; Chapter 15 › Main findings › Adult smokers’ and vapers’ harm perceptions of vaping in England, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 15 › Main findings › Interventions to change perceptions, 1st paragraph; Chapter 15 › Main findings › Vaping harm perceptions predicting changes in behaviour, 1st and 13th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusions (Chapter 16). The authors write that weaknesses in the choice of assessments and biomarkers, populations, groups and exposure, and study designs 'all limit the conclusions that we can draw'. They restate their 2015 statement that vaping 'is at least 95% less harmful than smoking' (smoking at least 20 times more harmful) and write that the estimate 'remains broadly accurate' at least over short term and medium term periods, while noting that summarising relative risks across products, behaviours and biomarkers 'can be simplistic and misinterpreted'; they suggest the statement that vaping poses 'only a small fraction of the risks of smoking' may be a better summary and repeat that vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked. They list 61 evidence statements (not printed on the pages read) that follow the National Academies' level definitions and involve 'a great deal of expert judgement'. Research recommendations include a common set of biomarkers, standard definitions of who is studied, agreed protocols and pre-registration. Implications: the authors say evidence from stop-smoking services and the Cochrane living review (not covered in their report) shows that vaping is effective for stopping smoking; higher absolute exposure than not using nicotine reinforces discouraging uptake by people who have never smoked; since the July 2021 cut-off new studies have been published, and the authors recommend a continual updating approach.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 16, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 16 › Overall findings in the context of our series of evidence reviews, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 16 › Evidence statements, 1st paragraph; Chapter 16 › Recommendations for research, 1st paragraph; Chapter 16 › Overall implications, 1st, 2nd and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Main findings page (a separate GOV.UK page). It calls the report 'the most comprehensive to date', with a main focus on 'a systematic review of the evidence on the health risks of nicotine vaping', and says it 'provides the most robust evidence on health risks of vaping to date'. Overall conclusions (four bullets): in the short and medium term vaping poses a small fraction of the risks of smoking; vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked; evidence is mostly limited to short and medium term effects and studies of vaping for more than 12 months are necessary; more standardised methods would improve interpretation. Biomarkers of toxicant exposure: significantly lower exposure to harmful substances from vaping than from smoking, as shown by biomarkers associated with the risk of cancer, respiratory and cardiovascular conditions; similar or higher exposure than from not using nicotine products; no significant increase of toxicant biomarkers after short-term secondhand exposure to vaping among people who do not smoke or vape. Biomarkers of potential harm: only limited conclusions could be drawn, but 'better-run studies' of short and medium term risks 'found no major causes of concern'. Vaping among adults who have never smoked 'remained very low' (0.6% to 0.7% in 2021).
key_findings.locator: Main findings page › 1. The review, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2. Health risks, 1st paragraph; 2.1 Overall conclusions, 1st to 4th bullets; 2.2 Biomarkers of toxicant exposure, 1st to 3rd bullets; 2.3 Biomarkers of potential harm, 2nd and 3rd sentences of the paragraph; 3.2 Adults, 3rd bullet

reporting_issues.issue: Follow-up beyond 12 months is described three ways. Chapter 7 says follow-up in the exposure review ran from 8 days to 12 months and that 'we were unable to summarise findings on longer term' vaping exposure. Chapter 5 cites 'medium to longer term studies (up to 2 years)' for nicotine exposure. Chapter 10 rates exposure as lower for vaping than smoking with moderate evidence at 'long-term exposure (more than 12 months)'. The studies behind the longer periods are not named on the pages read.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 7 › Evidence reviewed, 6th paragraph; Chapter 5 › Main findings › Nicotine intake, 4th paragraph; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Biomarkers of respiratory diseases, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: For follow-up length, the safe statement is that the pooled exposure analyses cover up to 12 months; any longer-term exposure result in the Summary needs the full report's tables before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 10 reports that spirometry showed no detrimental effects at acute, short-to-medium or long-term (more than 12 months) exposure. A few paragraphs later it concludes there is 'insufficient evidence' from spirometry, FeNO, oscillometry, bronchoscopy and imaging on whether vaping affects lung function at those durations. The first reads as a finding of no effect; the second says the studies cannot tell.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 10 › Main findings › Respiratory tests and imaging, 2nd and 6th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the insufficient-evidence conclusion for lung function. The no-detrimental-effects sentence describes what small, mostly short studies found; it is not evidence that there is no effect.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 10 says there was 'limited evidence that vaping negatively affects lung function among adults with asthma', but its Conclusions section says differences in designs, diagnoses and measurements in the asthma studies 'prevent us from making any conclusions'.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 10 › Main findings › Asthma, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Conclusions, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The asthma result is at most a limited signal of harm from 4 small studies; the Summary does not make clear whether its authors treat it as a conclusion.

reporting_issues.issue: The COPD section gives spirometry results from two articles drawn from one group of patients (small numbers) and then states 'limited evidence' for fewer COPD exacerbations; exacerbations are not among the results listed. The Conclusions add that improvements 'seem mainly to be among participants who switched to exclusive vaping', a subgroup finding. The Summary says the update is the 5-year follow-up reported 'by the same study group' that supplied the National Academies' limited-evidence conclusion, so it adds follow-up of one cohort, not a second cohort.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 10 › Main findings › Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Conclusions, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat COPD improvement after switching as one small cohort followed for up to 5 years, with spirometry results given and the exacerbation result not shown in the Summary.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 8 says larger studies found lower HDL cholesterol in people who use no nicotine than in people who vape and smoke; Chapter 11 says that in large samples HDL was significantly higher in people who use no nicotine than in people who vape and smoke. The studies are not named. Higher HDL in people who do not smoke is the usual direction, so Chapter 8 may have the direction reversed (reader's inference).
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 8 › Main findings › Oxidative stress, 3rd paragraph; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Cholesterol, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite neither sentence for the direction of HDL differences. Chapter 8's two pooled cross-sectional analyses, which found no difference in HDL between people who vape and either comparison group, are the only consistent statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The Main findings page says that 'better-run studies' of short and medium term risks 'found no major causes of concern'. The Summary does not say which studies were judged better run, how, or how many. Its chapters say most studies had methodological concerns (Chapters 7, 8, 10 and 11), rate lung-function evidence insufficient, and say most of the biomarker-of-harm studies 'cannot inform us about the medium or long term' risks.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 7 › Implications › Methodological improvements needed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 8 › Implications › Need to distinguish between biomarkers of potential harm from smoking or vaping from other sources, 1st paragraph; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Respiratory tests and imaging, 6th paragraph; Main findings page › 2.3 Biomarkers of potential harm, 3rd sentence of the paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: For biomarkers of potential harm, cite the chapter-level statements with their evidence levels, not the sentence about better-run studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 16 says the 'at least 95% less harmful' estimate 'remains broadly accurate' for the short and medium term. The pages read show no calculation from the review's results to that figure: the pooled reductions printed for individual exposure biomarkers run from 58% to 94%, nicotine exposure does not differ significantly from smoking in five pooled comparisons, some markers are higher than in people who use no nicotine, and no disease outcome is pooled. The authors themselves say such summaries 'can be simplistic and misinterpreted' and that their evidence levels involve 'a great deal of expert judgement'.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 16 › Overall findings in the context of our series of evidence reviews, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Tobacco specific nitrosamines, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Volatile organic compounds, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 16 › Evidence statements, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the figure as the authors' judgement, with their qualifiers (short and medium term; not risk-free), and not as a result of this review's analyses.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 8 concludes that switching 'might improve endothelial function in the longer-term'. The only supporting human study described is a single RCT of 4 weeks (Chapter 11 says 'after one month'). Chapter 11 says pulse wave velocity may improve after a sustained switch but 'the longest follow-up reported was only 4 months'. The Main findings page calls studies of vaping for more than 12 months necessary.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 8 › Main findings › Endothelial function, 3rd and 7th paragraphs; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Endothelial function, 1st paragraph; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Peripheral resistance and arterial stiffness, 1st paragraph; Main findings page › 2.1 Overall conclusions, 3rd bullet
reporting_issues.consequence: In this review 'longer-term' for these outcomes means 1 to 4 months, not the more than 12 months the authors elsewhere call necessary.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 16 refers to 61 evidence statements that are not printed on the pages read. Level words appear in the chapter text (for example 'conclusive evidence' of lower carcinogen exposure; substantial evidence of comparable nicotine exposure in experienced adults; moderate evidence of similar exposure up to 2 years) without the number of studies, designs or risk-of-bias ratings behind each, and the authors say the framework involves expert judgement.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 16 › Evidence statements, 1st paragraph; Chapter 5 › Main findings › Nicotine intake, 4th paragraph; Chapter 9 › Main findings › Cancer risks, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite a level word together with the counts and designs given in the same chapter, and check the numbered statement in the full report before relying on its wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The review's two questions, as printed in Chapters 7 and 10, concern biomarkers associated with the risk of disease and disease outcomes in people with existing conditions. Neither question asks about new disease in people who did not already have it. Chapter 11 nevertheless says that 'to date there is still no available evidence' on clinical cardiovascular outcomes. The Summary names no individual study, so it is unknown whether cohort or cross-sectional studies of heart or lung disease were searched for or excluded. A PATH Study cohort report of new respiratory conditions had been published before the July 2021 cut-off (card sc_xie_2020), and one on cardiovascular disease after it (card sc_berlowitz_2022).
